HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Parts of a Home (Outside) — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the outside of a home as a reading exercise: the house is the book, and the curb is the reading chair.

What is this?

From the outside a home shows the parts that face the world: the front door, the windows, the roof on top, the chimney that used to carry smoke, the garage that shelters the car.

What does it mean?

Outside parts are how children learn that homes come in kinds — with garages and without, flat roofs and pointy. "Some homes do, some don&rsquo;t" is the sentence this lesson plants.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and a window or doorstep with a view of any house. No walking required for round one; the street does the showing.

Why this matters

House-watching is calm, free and endlessly available. A child who can read a house&rsquo;s parts from a distance has a five-minute game that works in every neighborhood on Earth.

What it teaches

Observation from distance, comparison (this roof, that roof), and honest variation — the same word can fit different-looking homes.

Words to learn

front doorroofchimneygaragewindowoutside

Say this to your child

“"Parts of a home — outside! There is our front door, there is the roof sitting on top like a hat. Does our house have a chimney? Let us look!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "every part on this card is outside — let us spot them."
  2. From the window or step, find your own front door, then your roof.
  3. Hunt for a chimney (some houses have none — say so) and a garage.
  4. Count the windows you can see from where you stand.
  5. Next walk, repeat from the curb — a different house each time.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Parts of a Home" sit over a pale-blue front door, a four-pane window, a blue-tiled roof, a brick chimney and a garage with its door down.

Ask your child

"What is on top of the house?" (the roof) "Where does the car sleep?" (the garage — if there is one) "Which part do guests knock on?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might declare every roof a hat, ask why some chimneys are quiet, or point out garages for the whole length of the street.

Out in the real world

House-reading travels: on any drive, any walk, any storybook picture, the five outside parts are findable. Buildings in books get read with the same words.

Try it together

House I-Spy: "I spy with my little eye a part of a home that is red" — the roof, the door, whatever fits. Five finds wins; the winner picks the next house to read.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the roof do?" (sits on top, keeps the rain out) "Where does smoke come from when there is a fire?" (the chimney) "What part do we knock?" (the front door)

This lesson pairs with the Parts of a Home (Outside) flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.
